I do wonder what will happen when all the CRT TVs die; but that's really a silly problem for me to worry about at all, as, surely, they will outlast me by decades.

This conversation does remind me that I saw a TV from the 1940s at a local art museum this summer.  I looked the model up while I was there and I think it was made in something like 1947, but I can't be certain.  That TV didn't work; it was a hollow hulk used in an art display, but it did make me think, "Damn, television has been around a LONG time!"

I understand that videogame consoles required late-1960s/early 1970s electronics technology to be invented before a videogame system could be made, but I'd love to see an Atari 2600 or Astrocade being played on a B&W, 1950s model television.  The oldest TV that I have is a B&W, 5" portable TV from 1976.  It's a bit too small for videogame uses, but I keep it around because, one, I got it for just $5 a few years ago and, two, it's neat to play Pong on it.

Adam

I passed on Kevin's questions and here are the responses.

Kevin:  What did your friends and family think of the system generally and your games?

Dale: I'm sure that people thought it was a cheap knockoff of the Atari 2600. It wouldn’t surprise me if my parents got it because it was on sale :). Of course, when I first got it, I had no idea that it would be user-programmable. I actually don't recall getting any specific feedback on my games from friends and family at the time, though I'm sure that they were amused.

Kevin: Looking back, what do you think about the Bally Arcade as a game system and as a development platform?

Dale: I thought it was amazing at the time. Of course, writing programs using the small keypad with the screen constantly changing colours was challenging, but with only 1800 bytes to fill it wasn't too bad.

Kevin: What experiences, if any, did you have with arcades or games on other systems? Did anything from those serve as inspirations for anything you worked on?

Dale: I didn't have any other development experiences back then, game or otherwise; going to the arcade as a teenager was always fun and definitely inspired me to try to create my own games. After Astrogrames, I didn't really do any professional game development, but I would say that whatever inspired me to create Astrogrames in the first place "permanently" transformed me into a part-time tinkerer outside of normal work; some of my projects are shared here: https://github.com/gumbypp?tab=repositories. More recently, I have written a few simple games for a joytstick-enabled variant of https://github.com/gumbypp/PixArt and its successor (a 20x30 NeoPixel LED board), and also encouraged my son to do the same.

In some respects, I've come full circle as writing code in 2021 for a limited memory-constrained environment like the Arduino Uno is not unlike writing code for the Astrocde 35+ (!) years ago.

I also enjoy sharing my love of tinkering with kids. I've taught 3 middle school "Coding & Making" tech elective classes at my kids' middle school and had just started teaching the fourth when Covid shut everything down :(.

Kevin: Do you remember which of your tapes were the most popular?

I would guess Multi-Adventure, but I'm not really sure. Of course, I only sold 50-ish tapes in total, so the term “popular” is relative :)

Here is Michael's full description of the demo (available to read on YouTube).

----------------------------------------

MCM Design's modified for hi-res SRAM Astrocade has 128KB of static screen RAM for use with an onboard  hi-res 8 page multi-pager. An 8KB program was created to test the multi-pager, then execute a hi-res Fish Demo.

Below is a listing of the 8 pages indicating what graphics appear on each page.

Page     Hi-Res Graphics
   0         text introduction with 17 lines of custom 7 x 9 pixel text

   1         narrow vertical stripes on a split screen

   2         end view of aquarium plus 15 magic write variations

   3         narrow horizontal stripes on a split screen

   4         10 color textured test pattern

   5         narrow vertical plus horizontal stripes on a split screen

   6         title page with custom enlarged text characters

   7         custom screenshot variation of the game Gunfight


0:00   BEGIN EXECUTION OF THE HI-RES MULTIPAGE TEST DEMO

The text introduction will be displayed nearly 60 seconds allowing ample time to read the custom hi-res text characters written by an Astrocade computer.

The test demo writes 7 hi-res pages of graphics to pages 2 thru 7 while the page 0 text intro is displayed.

Several passes of the 8 page flipping will execute next. The speed of page flipping will increase with each pass. Each page flip produces an audio output.


3:34  CRITTER MOVES AROUND ERASING GRAPHICS IN ALL 8 PAGES

After the page flipping, you will see a critter moving around and erasing graphics in all of the 8 pages.

The 98 byte program that is executed to move the critter actually resides in the bottom of page 7. This program calls subroutines within the cassette cartridge ROM.

Audio comments are included during the motion of the critter.


7:38   HI-RES FISH DEMO

After the critter finishes erasing graphics in the last page, which is the custom Gunfight screenshot, the hi-res Fish Demo is executed for 2 minutes, followed by a loop back to the page 0 intro text.


9:39  EXECUTION OF THE MULTIPAGE TEST DEMO WITH NO MULTI-PAGER HARDWARE

If no multi-pager hardware is present, the multipage test demo will execute in the following manner.

All of the 8 page graphics will be visible but QUICKLY written ending in the final page Gunfight screenshot.
The screenshot colors will very with each audio output.
The color variation and audio output occurrence will increase over time.
A crash will likely occur at the end of the color/audio output variation or there will be a loop back to the quick 8 page graphics write.


12:31   MOVE CRITTER AROUND 3 PAGES (SCENES) USING A HAND CONTROLLER


Final Comments

When a page is flipped, there are no issues with any graphic pixels. However, there are 2 what could be described as video display disturbances.

The first occasional disturbance appears as a momentary long, but narrow white streak, typically on the right side of the screen RAM area and seems to be prominent in the page 7 Gunfight screenshot. It has been determined that this disturbance is related to the changing of colors. This disturbance is also seen when the test demo is executed with NO multi-pager hardware (see video clip at 9:39). This explanation was confirmed when the program was revised to use only 1 color table for all 8 pages. When only 1 color table was used, the noted disturbance was not present.

The second occasional disturbance cannot be described with words, but is easily visible. Perhaps this particular disturbance is related to a TV graphics display appearing abnormally fast. Normally, the TV display data in the screen RAM area has to be cleared, then the appropriate graphics has to written to screen RAM. MCM Design also tried running faster chips, but this second disturbance would still occur occasionally.


End Of Description
Sept 2021

18279:
When I converted my newsletter, Orphaned Computers & Game Systems (OC&GS), into pdf format back in the late 1990s, I used some tools that were available back then from various sources.  What's interesting is that these pdfs were put onto archive.org by Jason Scott back in 2013.  All twelve issues are here:

https://archive.org/details/orphanedcomputerandgame

The way I converted the last nine issues to pdf from my Amiga was that I output to a postscript file and then converted that using Adobe Distiller.  Perhaps issues of Slap Dash can be converted using this method.  My process sounds simple, but there were many utilities that I had to use in-between to glue the whole process together.  The first three issues of the newsletter were just regular scans because the issues were cut & paste together.

The OC&GS website still gets new articles now and then.  The most recent one is from December 2020:

https://orphanedgames.com/

The time of classic gaming newsletters was pretty short-lived; I'm glad that I was part of it.  Perhaps one day someone will write a book covering that period.

Adam

Hey, Matt.  Welcome to our small community.  As you have seen already, there aren't many different resources for the Astrocade, but the few that exist are full of fans who are ready to help. Starting off with the Atari 2600 as your first experience as a second-generation console is how I bet many people began playing videogames in the early 1980s.  That was the system to beat, and with good reason.  It had many arcade ports and the games are fun and easy to obtain.  The Bally Arcade wasn't easy to find and its game library was small.  The system had overheating problems and the three companies that sold the various versions of the console eventually gave up on it.  It passed from one parent to another after a year or two.  Each company seems like they actually did try their best to get the console out to consumers, but due to various complications, few people have experienced this system.

I'm glad that you find BASIC for the system intriguing.  Since you are an experienced programmer in both your professional and hobby life, maybe you will jump in and get your hands dirty programming in either Z80 assembly language or AstroBASIC.  All of the material that you need is on ballyalley.com.  If you need some help, then throw up a hand here and someone will call on you promptly.

Greetings all!

I’m excited to be part of this group and wanted to share a quick introduction. I’ve been heavily interested in 2nd generation consoles and home computers for many years now (especially late-70s through mid-80s). The only 2nd gen console I experienced growing up was an Atari 2600. Over time I learned about and acquired other popular game consoles from the era (Intellivision, Colecovision, Odyssey) but hold much more intrigue and appreciation for the underdogs and largely forgotten systems of the day, especially the Bally.

My discovery of Bally began when I was searching out podcasts built around Z80-based architectures to listen to on long road trips. I hold a bias toward Z80 powered machines simply because I have a lot more familiarity with that architecture and my other most beloved obscure platform is the Z80-based Mattel Aquarius, which only survived in the market for a few months before being axed. My searches led to the discovery of Adam’s Bally Alley podcast and the amazing wealth of information preserved on the website about a system that otherwise could’ve been largely lost to history. The more I learned about the system the more impressed I was. I’ve enjoyed listening to the podcasts and sifting through the abundance of materials about this unique and very capable platform. It was fun to review the origins of the Arcadian newsletter and all of the anticipation the contributors had back then to the release of Bally BASIC—and rightfully so. I am a computer programmer both by profession and as a hobbyist and am most drawn to the development and technical capabilities of the Bally.

I imagine how incredible it must had felt to the lucky owners of the Bally back in the day with the debut of BASIC. This was not just a gimmick “make your own game in minutes” sort of cartridge or novelty that some platforms had, but instead offered a full-blown implementation of BASIC complete with save/load  capabilities via cassette (both the 300 and 2000 baud variants). Had I grown up at the time and been treated to this sort of revolution to a system that I initially expected was only to play games on, there’s no doubt I would’ve spent many months mastering the syntax and creating a lot of programs for my own enjoyment and to share with others. The features of its BASIC implementation are leaps and bounds more complete than other dedicated platforms; this includes the aforementioned Aquarius, which released 5 years later as a home computer but still lacked most things that the Bally offered (Aquarius contained only a 80x72 drawable view, 16 colors, no GPU, a fixed character ROM, no built-in BASIC commands to handle graphics or interface with joysticks/multi-voice sound found on the expander).

With many thanks to Allen Schweitzer and his devotion toward Bally restoration and preservation, I am now the owner of a functional physical machine. I avoided emulating any aspects of the system until I had a physical one to use, since I wanted my entire experience to be organic just as it would’ve felt back in the day. Bally’s games are highly impressive and I am still just starting to work my way through the library. Both the visuals and sound effects seem directly comparable to an authentic arcade experience from that time period. The controllers are really innovative and fun to use given the multi-purpose of the analog stick unlike anything I’ve seen before. The first night I had it operating my mom visited and we both had a blast playing the integrated Gunfight game, which was one of the first games my mom had played since Stampede on the Atari 2600! It was tremendous fun and we got a lot of laughs out of it.

Last night I played the Bally BASIC demonstration program and just watching that and seeing the potential even just in BASIC alone was fascinating and again I imagine how intriguing this would had been to Bally owners back in the day, when suddenly a full programmable computer was at their fingertips (even if the planned keyboard/PC accessories never came to fruition). I also have dabbled into Z80 machine language for other platforms and look forward to development efforts and experimentation with the Bally for years to come.

Thank you all!

Matt

https://ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html#BalCheckHRAstrocadeROMImage

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/BallyCheck/BallyCheck.html#BalcheckHRUserManual

The following two email exchanges that Michael Matte had with Allen and me, is working on an astrocade motherboard that fails.  He designates this board as BD7.  Whenever Michael refers to "you" or "your," he is referring to Allen.

Michael talks about how he substitutes a Z80 that is not connected to the Astrocade motherboard and yet it allows it to run on the Astrocade motherboard.  This uses hardware that is Michael's own design.  He does not plan to create it for others, even though he has been offered the opportunity to, perhaps, have this is design placed on a professional-grade PCB.

These two pieces of email give a behind-the-scene look at the process that Michael uses to diagnose a regular astrocade (a non-hi-res console) using a tool he originally designed for his hi-res unit.

Adam

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Wednesday, July 21, 2021 9:33 PM
To: Allen S. and Adam T.
Subject: ALLEN BD7

I installed a Z80 and 74LS367 in my upgraded BalcheckHR breadboard. This breadboard was shown on my first YouTube video.  I checked all the applicable wiring on the breadboard and wiring to my connected working motherboard.

My remote Z80 substitution idea works. I used my logic probe to confirm the motherboard Z80 was tri-stated off.

I connected the breadboard to your failed Allen BD7, which will crash about 8 seconds after the menu powers on. Your board is now working great, when operated by the Z80 that's on my BalcheckHR board. How about that? The Z80 WAS acting up. The logic probe pulsing at the Custom Address RAS0 output line is now pulsing normally. My suspicion was correct about this irregularity when I compared my working motherboard with your failed motherboard. I'm finding out that my logic probe is becoming a very powerful diagnostic tool.

I'm going to let you replace the Z80 because you have the proper tool and the skills for replacing such a big chip.

I have an address chip that runs perfect in low-res, but has an issue in hi-res. I would like permission to test your address chip in ALLEN BD7 to see if it runs perfect in hi-res. From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, August 5, 2021 6:53 PM
To: Allen S.
Cc: Adam T.
Subject: Allen BD1 
 
Man, I've been experiencing Astrocade motherboard failures lately. My Allen BD1 had a failure recently.  The board powered on with a black screen and the Z80 Check program wouldn't execute. I thought maybe I killed the Z80 when I was using this board to test my new Remote Z80 diagnostic board. Turns out there was no negated 7M clock. This clock was not present at the Kludge board pin 1. Since the regular 7M clock was ok, I knew the crystal and transistor Q2 were ok. I never worked in this area of the motherboard before this failure.

- Found a way to remove all that RF shielding surrounding the Kludge board area. 

- Desoldered the Kludge board.

- Desoldered U16.

- Soldered in the two 8 and 16 pin pc sockets you gave me. These were really nice sockets in that they had metal contacts on their bottoms to help make contact with the top motherboard solder pads. Do you remember where you purchased these sockets?

- Installed new SN75361AP and 74S74 chips.

- Soldered in a new crystal since the original was very old.

The motherboard works great again. Yippy! Now there are only 3 chips on this board with no sockets. Nice! I plan to use this board as a low-res test board and also as my final "modified for hi-res" motherboard. It's a dual-purpose board. Cool!

Bye.
MCM

Some time ago, my hi-res SRAM Astrocade failed. The last several days, because I was making great progress in restoring the Astrocade, I decided to try and finish this project. I'm happy to report the hi-res SRAM Astrocade is up and running great again.

I tested your first of 6 custom address chips you mailed me, per our agreement, and found it to be operating perfect in both low and hi-res modes.

So you know exactly what I am doing with your chips, here is my detailed test procedure.

- Enter hobby room with shoes off.
- Touch metal light fixture before handling motherboard or components.
- Check custom address chip for bent pins.
- Clean dull pins using used 400 grit wet/dry sandpaper.
- Carefully install chip in socket. Use fingers to align pins if necessary.
- Make sure chip is all the way down into socket.
- Visually check all 40 pins for a bent pin.
- Double check 40 pins for good socket connections using an ohmmeter. Note: It is possible (low risk) during installation for the tip of a pin to be bent inward and under the chip.
- Use Bally schematic and MCM large data chip diagram to check all 40 pins for a good (zero ohm) connection. It takes nearly 20 minutes to perform this test.
MCM Design recommendation: Perform ohmmeter check test to confirm a perfect custom chip installation.

Place MCM temporary custom black finned heat sink with Si grease on top of the address chip.
This chip can heat up pretty warm when running in hi-res for a long period of time.

Use 6" fan to help dissipate heat radiating at address/data chips and power supply components.
This cooling option might extend the lifespan of the data chips, Q1 transistor or voltage regulators, which may not have internal thermal protection.
I have seen in the past, the custom address/data chips cease functioning when they got too hot, then function again when cooled down.

Run the following programs to test for a crash or graphic glitches.
Do power on motherboard 2 or 3 times to run all tests.
Any power on issues?

HI-RES MODE

- Original hi-res test demo*
- Watch entire multi-page demo (19 minute program)
- Hi-res 12 fish (magic writes) demo*
- Hi-res screen RAM test (will stop running if RAM error is detected)
- Test pattern variation (watch several passes)
- Low-res Checkmate on a hi-res map (run a few rounds to see if it will crash)

LOW-RES MODE

- BalcheckHR Checkmate variation, 100 rounds nonstop (crash test only)
- BalcheckHR fish demo**
- Balcheck nonstop test ** (will stop running if RAM error is detected)

*   Run at least 60 minutes
** Run at least 30 minutes

Label chip as an address chip and include MCM low and hi-res status assessments (GOOD or ISSUE).

Bye.
MCM

Hi Ken. It just occurred to me that your one SRAM chip idea may work if you wanted to multi-page the low-res mode. However, in the hi-res mode, at least 4 SRAM chips are required because of the way the hi-res mode map is fed into the data chip. Four 74LS166 chips are needed to serially feed the map into the data chip via the SERIAL 0 and SERIAL 1 inputs. Each of the 4 chips has 8 lines wired to screen RAM data outputs, totaling 32 lines for the data out serial feed.

I still would like to see a sketch of your idea. Once I see your idea in my head, I might be able to use a variation of the idea.

A new idea I have is to feed the output of IC6 in DWG3, which senses when all 4 RAS lines are high for the video scan feed, through an inverter and then to the four 74LS245 enable pins, which should disable the 4 chips from the 4 video data buses during the video scan. Then feed the DATEN line to a decoder to direct the appropriate video data bus for the Z80 screen RAM read or the magic OR, XOR function read. This idea is similar to the 74LS253 application in the hi-res DRAM scheme. I might have to tweak this idea. Anyway, this is an idea I will definitely experiment with.

It looks like the Z80 would be able to write to or read from your hi-res SRAM scheme. However, the scheme is not compatible with the custom chip hi-res video display scan (read).

You should check out DWG 6, which is archived at

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html

Scroll down near the bottom to view DWGs 1 thru 6.

DWG 6 shows the entire video display scanning scheme with an overview commentary. There are also some DWG 6 comments just before DWG 1. The commentary will also point you to a doc with an in depth description of the custom address/data chip operation in low or hi-res modes, including the hi-res video display scan. The Nutting Manual system description also provides some info.

I could hook up my Kingst LA and save a hi-res sampling that would show the video scan wave forms. I could run my short "Z80 Halt" program, so all you'll see on the sampling are the wave forms related to the hi-res video scan. This program will halt the Z80 so it will just execute NOPs. The Z80 will not write to or read from the screen RAM when halted. Apparently, the video scan also doubles as a DRAM row address refresh, so you probably wouldn't even see an independent refresh attempt in the sampling. I think, if I emailed the saved sampling file, you would be able to view it. Let me know if you would like me to email you a sampling of the custom chip's hi-res video display scanning.

My failed hi-res SRAM Astrocade is now up and running great again. This is the Astrocade with the hi-res 128KB, 8 page multi-pager. I now have 2 working modified for hi-res motherboards with a 28 pin dual in line ribbon cable socket mounted on the bottom front of the motherboard. My hi-res DRAM Astrocade utilizes a 24 pin socket.

I have begun work on my final hi-res Astrocade which will have 3 add under boards along with a provision for a 4th board. There will be a sliding horizontal rack for boards 2, 3 and 4. I'm utilizing a customized 7 x 8.5" quick connect breadboard first for board 1, so I can make quick changes to run various tests.

The breadboard 1 will only have the screen SRAM and its interfacing. I am expecting to have this board running in low-res within a week.

I broke down the Perkin's interface schematic into 3 schematics so the interfacing scheme is easier to read. My quick connect breadboard 1 will be used to further my Perkin's investigation and run "Perkin tests".

My DWG 5, as documented on the Bally Alley, is set up for a manual low or hi-res selection.

Yes, Michael is right, "[Trying to get homebrew ] games going on the Astrocade is like capturing fairy dust or something."

It isn't that there isn't excitement about the Astrocade for potential cartridge homebrew programmers, but these people run into several issues when trying to program for the Astrocade:

- The Astrocade emulation in MAME is weak: it's not cycle accurate, the speed isn't quite right and the colors are off, and in some cases wrong.

- Getting a working Astrocade is difficult.

- Keeping an Astrocade working isn't easy.

I'm not sure what the future holds in the emulation area for the Astrocade, but there is plenty that can be done with only 8K of ROM and an unexpanded system.

Adam

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, August 5, 2021 6:53 PM
To: Allen S.
Cc: Adam T.
Subject: Allen BD1

Man, I've been experiencing Astrocade motherboard failures lately. My Allen BD1 had a failure recently.  The board powered on with a black screen and the Z80 Check program wouldn't execute. I thought maybe I killed the Z80 when I was using this board to test my new Remote Z80 diagnostic board. Turns out there was no negated 7M clock. This clock was not present at the Kludge board pin 1. Since the regular 7M clock was ok, I knew the crystal and transistor Q2 were ok. I never worked in this area of the motherboard before this failure.

- Found a way to remove all that RF shielding surrounding the Kludge board area.

- Desoldered the Kludge board.

- Desoldered U16.

- Soldered in the two 8 and 16 pin pc sockets you gave me. These were really nice sockets in that they had metal contacts on their bottoms to help make contact with the top motherboard solder pads. Do you remember where you purchased these sockets?

- Installed new SN75361AP and 74S74 chips.

- Soldered in a new crystal since the original was very old.

The motherboard works great again. Yippy! Now there are only 3 chips on this board with no sockets. Nice! I plan to use this board as a low-res test board and also as my final "modified for hi-res" motherboard. It's a dual-purpose board. Cool!

Bye.

Man, I've been experiencing Astrocade motherboard failures lately. My Allen BD1 had a failure recently.  The board powered on with a black screen and the Z80 Check program wouldn't execute. I thought maybe I killed the Z80 when I was using this board to test my new Remote Z80 diagnostic board. Turns out there was no negated 7M clock. This clock was not present at the Kludge board pin 1. Since the regular 7M clock was ok, I knew the crystal and transistor Q2 were ok. I never worked in this area of the motherboard before this failure.

- Found a way to remove all that RF shielding surrounding the Kludge board area.

- Desoldered the Kludge board.

- Desoldered U16.

- Soldered in the two 8 and 16 pin pc sockets you gave me. These were really nice sockets in that they had metal contacts on their bottoms to help make contact with the top motherboard solder pads. Do you remember where you purchased these sockets?

- Installed new SN75361AP and 74S74 chips.

- Soldered in a new crystal since the original was very old.

The motherboard works great again. Yippy! Now there are only 3 chips on this board with no sockets. Nice! I plan to use this board as a low-res test board and also as my final "modified for hi-res" motherboard. It's a dual-purpose board. Cool!

Bye.

If I could go back in time, then after buying Apple stock and some factory sealed Nintendo games, I would tell people to label their tapes better. Nate Reeder kindly loaned me some tapes, and one of these was originally Elvis' Worldwide Gold Award Hits, but all music has been erased, and it has a piece of tape on it that says only "10A". There's a lot of Astrocade data on there. The majority we already have archived from official tapes, but two programs I don't recognize. Perhaps I've played them before and forgotten, maybe they're newsletter programs, maybe they're unarchived commercial tapes, or maybe they were never published at all. I'll describe them and attach some files (processed recordings, BASIC code, and screenshots), and if anyone can offer more information, let me know.

The first program flashes "The Guard" in large font at the start, so that's what I'm calling it. You can move the character sprite up and down with the joystick. The screen wraps at the top and bottom. You can fire left or right with the joystick. Enemies approach from the side, which you can shoot to gain oxygen. Sometimes lasers fire at you from the side. Occasionally, obstacles pop up along your path that you have to avoid, or more helpfully extra oxygen pickups. You lose a life when you get hit or run out of oxygen.

In the second program, you control a flying saucer. There are targets on the ground that fire upon you. You need to shoot them first. Use the joystick to fly, and the trigger to shoot. You shoot directly down when stationary, or angled to the left or right when moving left or right. When you clear all targets, you get bonus points and the next round starts with a higher number of targets.

Not sure if it helps, but the identified programs found on the same tape are quite a mix of mostly commercial programs: Exitor's Revenge by L&M Software, Alien Invasion by L&M Software, The Gate Escape Side 1 by WaveMakers, Lookout For The Bull by WaveMakers, Gaswell Bonanza by Joe Peoples, and Micro Pac by H.A.R.D.

Paul

There is a Mister FPGA core for the Bally Arcade that is reasonably okay, though it is in need of updates - the author and I talked a while back, and they were not aware of the RAM expansions or audio interfaces for cassette programs, so both of those will need to be added (though they believe it would be a relatively easy addition, they just don't have the time at the moment). There have also been a few other quality of life developments since that core was created, such as very good RF filters etc. that it could take advantage of (and of course, if we can get a copy of the BIOS, the ZGRASS expansion could be added too).
Given the cost of FPGAs perfecting that kind of thing is probably the better approach vs trying to develop drop-in replacements that use FPGAs.

The first program flashes "The Guard" in large font at the start, so that's what I'm calling it. You can move the character sprite up and down with the joystick. You shoot directly down when stationary, or angled to the left or right when moving left or right. When you clear all targets, you get bonus points and the next round starts with a higher number of targets.

Not sure if it helps, but the identified programs found on the same tape are quite a mix of mostly commercial programs: Exitor's Revenge by L&M Software, Alien Invasion by L&M Software, The Gate Escape Side 1 by WaveMakers, Lookout For The Bull by WaveMakers, Gaswell Bonanza by Joe Peoples, and Micro Pac by H.A.R.D.

Yes, Michael is right, "[Trying to get homebrew ] games going on the Astrocade is like capturing fairy dust or something."

It isn't that there isn't excitement about the Astrocade for potential cartridge homebrew programmers, but these people run into several issues when trying to program for the Astrocade:

- The Astrocade emulation in MAME is weak: it's not cycle accurate, the speed isn't quite right and the colors are off, and in some cases wrong.

- Getting a working Astrocade is difficult.

- Keeping an Astrocade working isn't easy.

I'm not sure what the future holds in the emulation area for the Astrocade, but there is plenty that can be done with only 8K of ROM and an unexpanded system.

Adam

Its really a shame, to be honest.  I guess in a parallel dimension somewhere things might have gone different and someone is enjoying BRON, BalZerk, Hysteria, Borf or RoBaltron: 2084...

During the first week of August, Michael fixed a hard-to-find issue with an Astrocade board that he was repairing.  Here are the two email that he sent to Allen and me about it.

Adam

----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, August 5, 2021 6:53 PM
To: Allen S.
Cc: Adam T.
Subject: Allen BD1

Man, I've been experiencing Astrocade motherboard failures lately. My Allen BD1 had a failure recently.  The board powered on with a black screen and the Z80 Check program wouldn't execute. I thought maybe I killed the Z80 when I was using this board to test my new Remote Z80 diagnostic board. Turns out there was no negated 7M clock. This clock was not present at the Kludge board pin 1. Since the regular 7M clock was ok, I knew the crystal and transistor Q2 were ok. I never worked in this area of the motherboard before this failure.

- Found a way to remove all that RF shielding surrounding the Kludge board area.

- Desoldered the Kludge board.

- Desoldered U16.

- Soldered in the two 8 and 16 pin pc sockets you gave me. These were really nice sockets in that they had metal contacts on their bottoms to help make contact with the top motherboard solder pads. Do you remember where you purchased these sockets?

- Installed new SN75361AP and 74S74 chips.

- Soldered in a new crystal since the original was very old.

The motherboard works great again. Yippy! Now there are only 3 chips on this board with no sockets. Nice! I plan to use this board as a low-res test board and also as my final "modified for hi-res" motherboard. It's a dual-purpose board. Cool!

Bye.
MCM

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, August 5, 2021 6:58 PM
To: Adam T.
Subject: Second Modified For Hi-Res Motherboard.

Good news! My second modified for hi-res motherboard is up and running perfect in low-res. This board killed 2 custom address chips. Man, I hate losing a custom chip to a failure. That sucks.

Bye.
MCM

If I could go back in time, then after buying Apple stock and some factory sealed Nintendo games, I would tell people to label their tapes better. Nate Reeder kindly loaned me some tapes, and one of these was originally Elvis' Worldwide Gold Award Hits, but all music has been erased, and it has a piece of tape on it that says only "10A". There's a lot of Astrocade data on there. The majority we already have archived from official tapes, but two programs I don't recognize. Perhaps I've played them before and forgotten, maybe they're newsletter programs, maybe they're unarchived commercial tapes, or maybe they were never published at all. I'll describe them and attach some files (processed recordings, BASIC code, and screenshots), and if anyone can offer more information, let me know.

The first program flashes "The Guard" in large font at the start, so that's what I'm calling it. You can move the character sprite up and down with the joystick. The screen wraps at the top and bottom. You can fire left or right with the joystick. Enemies approach from the side, which you can shoot to gain oxygen. Sometimes lasers fire at you from the side. Occasionally, obstacles pop up along your path that you have to avoid, or more helpfully extra oxygen pickups. You lose a life when you get hit or run out of oxygen.

In the second program, you control a flying saucer. There are targets on the ground that fire upon you. You need to shoot them first. Use the joystick to fly, and the trigger to shoot. You shoot directly down when stationary, or angled to the left or right when moving left or right. When you clear all targets, you get bonus points and the next round starts with a higher number of targets.

Not sure if it helps, but the identified programs found on the same tape are quite a mix of mostly commercial programs: Exitor's Revenge by L&M Software, Alien Invasion by L&M Software, The Gate Escape Side 1 by WaveMakers, Lookout For The Bull by WaveMakers, Gaswell Bonanza by Joe Peoples, and Micro Pac by H.A.R.D.

Paul

18358:
"Space Game," as titled by Paul Thacker, seems to be the AstroBASIC version with machine language graphics of "Lazer Blazer."  This version was sold for $6 by Super Software (Rob Rosenhouse).  There is a simplified, "BOX" graphics-only (no ML graphics used) version that was printed in ARCADIAN 5, no. 6 (Apr. 4, 1983): 102-103.

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_5/arcadian_vol_5_issue_06.pdf

The full instructions for the BASIC-only version printed in the "Arcadian" are here:

"Lazer Blazer is a game of skill. The object is to destroy each of the lazer outposts before being hit yourself. The game uses joystick one. To move your spaceship, move the joystick in that direction. To fire straight down, pull the trigger. To fire at an angle, pull the trigger AND move the joystick at the same time. The first round consists of three bases. When you destroy all of them, you will receive bonus points, and will go on to the next round. If you take too long to complete a round, you will hear a warning sound. After the warning sound, you will only have a few seconds with which to hit the remaining base(s). Each game consists of three turns, with a bonus turn awarded at each interval of 2,500 points.

"The graphics in this game are simple 'BOX' graphics. A version of this game complete with machine language graphics is available from SUPER SOFTWARE for only $6.00.

"GOOD LUCK!!!"

There also appears to have been a version of the game for Blue Ram BASIC with extra features.  The BRB version is advertised in ARCADIAN 5, no. 6 (Apr. 4, 1983): 103.  The ad says:

"Tape BR 1 - Lazer Blazer - With the added memory of the Blue Ram, SUPER SOFTWARE has created a really SUPER version of the game published in the Arcadian. Among the other features included is a docking sequence. The lazer bases even move. At last, true animation in BASIC. ONLY $18.00 - It's a Blast!

None of these versions of "Lazer Blazer" seems to have ever been archived in any form before now.  Paul has done a great job unearthing this ultra-rare game from, of all places, a copy found on an Elvis tape!

Note that this is not the same game as the similarly titled "Laser Blazer" by W&W Software Sales.

Adam

"Space Game," as titled by Paul Thacker, seems to be the AstroBASIC version with machine language graphics of "Lazer Blazer."  This version was sold for $6 by Super Software (Rob Rosenhouse).  There is a simplified, "BOX" graphics-only (no ML graphics used) version that was printed in ARCADIAN 5, no. 6 (Apr. 4, 1983): 102-103.

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_5/arcadian_vol_5_issue_06.pdf

The full instructions for the BASIC-only version printed in the "Arcadian" are here:

"Lazer Blazer is a game of skill. The object is to destroy each of the lazer outposts before being hit yourself. The game uses joystick one. To move your spaceship, move the joystick in that direction. To fire straight down, pull the trigger. To fire at an angle, pull the trigger AND move the joystick at the same time. The first round consists of three bases. When you destroy all of them, you will receive bonus points, and will go on to the next round. If you take too long to complete a round, you will hear a warning sound. After the warning sound, you will only have a few seconds with which to hit the remaining base(s). Each game consists of three turns, with a bonus turn awarded at each interval of 2,500 points.

"The graphics in this game are simple 'BOX' graphics. A version of this game complete with machine language graphics is available from SUPER SOFTWARE for only $6.00.

"GOOD LUCK!!!"

There also appears to have been a version of the game for Blue Ram BASIC with extra features.  The BRB version is advertised in ARCADIAN 5, no. 6 (Apr. 4, 1983): 103.  The ad says:

"Tape BR 1 - Lazer Blazer - With the added memory of the Blue Ram, SUPER SOFTWARE has created a really SUPER version of the game published in the Arcadian. Among the other features included is a docking sequence. The lazer bases even move. At last, true animation in BASIC. ONLY $18.00 - It's a Blast!

None of these versions of "Lazer Blazer" seems to have ever been archived in any form before now.  Paul has done a great job unearthing this ultra-rare game from, of all places, a copy found on an Elvis tape!

Note that this is not the same game as the similarly titled "Laser Blazer" by W&W Software Sales.

Adam

I have added game descriptions for Super Software's Bally BASIC, 300-baud programs.  I also added a screenshot of the video art programs called "Diamonds."

These descriptions and details have been primarily taken from three sources:

1) Brief overviews (SOURCEBOOK, Fall 1980).
2) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Summer 1982)
3) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Spring 1984)

Previously, this software section of twenty programs (mostly from Super Software's first nine tapes) was a plain list of program names with links to the archived versions of the 300-baud software. Now each program has a brief description with some history as to the source of the program.

I've also added the three names and descriptions of the unarchived games that were released in 300-baud format from Tape 10 (Falling Stars and Laser Battle) and Tape 11 (Space Dock).  All of the other tapes (numbers 12-22) are only available as AstroBASIC games.  Tape BR1 and BR2 are Blue Ram BASIC games.  Most, perhaps all, of the games on Tapes 1-11 were also available in AstroBASIC format.

Interesting, the AstroBASIC game "Lazer Blazer," which was recently archived by Paul as an unknown game dubbed "Space Game" (but which appeared in Arcadian with an advanced version available on tape) does not seem to be listed by name in any of the advertised Tapes 1-22.  Perhaps the name "Lazer Blazer" was changed from an earlier name.  This renaming seems to be something of a trademark of Super Software; I wonder why this did it.

This is one of the  best updates in a long time. Thanks for spending the time updating all of this! I am looking forward to some Astrocade game playing this Friday!
    On Tuesday, October 5, 2021, 06:43:05 PM EDT, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:  
 
  I have added game descriptions for Super Software's Bally BASIC, 300-baud programs.  I also added a screenshot of the video art programs called "Diamonds."

These descriptions and details have been primarily taken from three sources:

1) Brief overviews (SOURCEBOOK, Fall 1980).
2) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Summer 1982)
3) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Spring 1984)

Previously, this software section of twenty programs (mostly from Super Software's first nine tapes) was a plain list of program names with links to the archived versions of the 300-baud software. Now each program has a brief description with some history as to the source of the program.

I've also added the three names and descriptions of the unarchived games that were released in 300-baud format from Tape 10 (Falling Stars and Laser Battle) and Tape 11 (Space Dock).  All of the other tapes (numbers 12-22) are only available as AstroBASIC games.  Tape BR1 and BR2 are Blue Ram BASIC games.  Most, perhaps all, of the games on Tapes 1-11 were also available in AstroBASIC format.

Interesting, the AstroBASIC game "Lazer Blazer," which was recently archived by Paul as an unknown game dubbed "Space Game" (but which appeared in Arcadian with an advanced version available on tape) does not seem to be listed by name in any of the advertised Tapes 1-22.  Perhaps the name "Lazer Blazer" was changed from an earlier name.  This renaming seems to be something of a trademark of Super Software; I wonder why this did it.

The section of 300-baud, Bally BASIC programs from Super Software is here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Super_Software/Super_Software.html
It was fun to spruce this section up.  Now it's time to play some of these Bally BASIC games from Super Software which Paul Thacker archived back in 2010.  Man, time just slips through my fingers; I've meant to look at these titles from years.  Has the time finally arrived where I'll give each game a bit of my time?  Does anyone else want to wander through this section and try the games with me?

Does anyone have any Super Software titles in AstroBASIC format?  Hardly any of these have been archived, which is a shame.
Below is the complete list of Super Software's Bally BASIC titles with descriptions.  

Adam

18373:
Anthony asked what the following statement might mean:

RND(11)b5-35

The printers back then couldn't print the multiply sign (at least not easily through the Bally BASIC kludge printer interface).  Thus, a lowercase "b" is the multiply sign.  So, the previous line would be (where my lowercase x is the multiply sign):

RND(11)x5-35

If I got this right, then a quick interpretation means a random number from 1 to 11 x 5 - 35.  Thus, the range is -30 to 30.  Hopefully that's right.

The Arcadian 10 Program Sampler explains how to read Bally BASIC printed listings on page 15 of the document:

http://mail.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_misc/arcadian-10_programs.pdf#Page=15

Also, the AstroBASIC manual is here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/Astro_BASIC_Manual_(instructions)(bally)(color)(300%20dpi).pdf

Anthony, I don't expect you to type in Laser Battle.  Let's make sure it's not available on some tape SOMEPLACE first.

So... Paul-- or anyone-- do you have Super Software's "Laser Battle" on tape?

Adam

On Tue, Oct 5, 2021 at 6:43 PM Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com<mailto:ballyalley@hotmail.com><mailto:ballyalley@hotmail.com<mailto:ballyalley@hotmail.com>>> wrote:
I have added game descriptions for Super Software's Bally BASIC, 300-baud programs.  I also added a screenshot of the video art programs called "Diamonds."

These descriptions and details have been primarily taken from three sources:

1) Brief overviews (SOURCEBOOK, Fall 1980).
2) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Summer 1982)
3) Advertisements (SOURCEBOOK, Spring 1984)

Previously, this software section of twenty programs (mostly from Super Software's first nine tapes) was a plain list of program names with links to the archived versions of the 300-baud software. Now each program has a brief description with some history as to the source of the program.

I've also added the three names and descriptions of the unarchived games that were released in 300-baud format from Tape 10 (Falling Stars and Laser Battle) and Tape 11 (Space Dock).  All of the other tapes (numbers 12-22) are only available as AstroBASIC games.  Tape BR1 and BR2 are Blue Ram BASIC games.  Most, perhaps all, of the games on Tapes 1-11 were also available in AstroBASIC format.

Interesting, the AstroBASIC game "Lazer Blazer," which was recently archived by Paul as an unknown game dubbed "Space Game" (but which appeared in Arcadian with an advanced version available on tape) does not seem to be listed by name in any of the advertised Tapes 1-22.  Perhaps the name "Lazer Blazer" was changed from an earlier name.  This renaming seems to be something of a trademark of Super Software; I wonder why this did it.

The section of 300-baud, Bally BASIC programs from Super Software is here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Super_Software/Super_Software.html

It was fun to spruce this section up.  Now it's time to play some of these Bally BASIC games from Super Software which Paul Thacker archived back in 2010.  Man, time just slips through my fingers; I've meant to look at these titles from years.  Has the time finally arrived where I'll give each game a bit of my time?  Does anyone else want to wander through this section and try the games with me?

Does anyone have any Super Software titles in AstroBASIC format?  Hardly any of these have been archived, which is a shame.

Below is the complete list of Super Software's Bally BASIC titles with descriptions.

Adam

----------

Bally Football.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 2, Side 1.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

This game was later renamed to just "Football."

"Now you can play the hand-held version of football on your Bally. Includes more features than its electronic counterpart. Two players."

"Play the famous hand-held version of football on your Astrocade computer. Guide your receiver into the end zone and score a touchdown."

----------

Bally Slot.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 5, Side 1.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

This game was later renamed "Astro Slot."

"A real slot machine is displayed on your television. See how lucky you are by spinning the reels graphically and see the results. This game is very realistic, as the IRS man comes to claim your winnings."

"Bally draws a real slot machine on the screen!! It's totally animated! Lively win schedule. But watch out for the IRS if you win too much."

"'Astro Slot' draws a real slot machine in two colors on your screen. Pull the trigger to set the reels in motion. Payoffs are according to the outcome."

----------

Barricade (Version 4.0).
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 8, Side 1.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"You have been imprisoned within the confines of an immense dungeon. Five furious fiends frantically frighten you into frenzied flight. The sole intention of these fiends is to electrocute you. How long can you survive against their relentless assault?"

----------

Beatle Quiz.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 3, Side 2 (SOURCEBOOK, Fall 1980).
Tape 7, Side 1 (SOURCEBOOK, Summer 1982).
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"In Beatle Quiz, test yourself on the Fab Four."

"See to what degree of Beatle-mania you really are by answering all the questions the BALLY gives you."

----------

Cosmic Zap.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 8, Side 2.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"In Cosmic Zap, you must protect your space station from meteor showers which strike from the north, south, east and west. Use your laser weapon to destroy the meteors. Frying Fee: $10.00."

----------

Diamonds.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
ARCADIAN 3, no. 9 (Jul. 09, 1981): 93.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

This short, type-in, BASIC program creates video art.

----------

Dog Races.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 5, Side 2.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

In ads for this game, this title is called "Dog Racing."

"It's off to the Bally track for a night of Dog Racing. Four people place their bets and the dogs fly across the track. All bets are displayed."

"Up to 4 people can bet on this fast paced dog race. Each player bets, then the race is on! All action displayed with graphics!"

"Dog Racing lets up to four people bet on the results of a dog race featuring five graphic dogs. Watch as the dogs fight to cross the finish line. Great fun!"

----------

Falling Stars. - NOT YET ARCHIVED
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 10, Side 1.
1981.

"Radioactive meteorites are descending on a major metropolitan city. The city's only protection is a weak shield and your limited laser weapon (you are supplied with one gallon per round). Once an area of the shield becomes damaged, the city is vulnerable. Do your best to save the city for as long as you can."

----------

Guided Missile.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 6, Side 1.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

According to Mike White's list of Astrocade software, this game seems to have been later renamed to "Missile Attack."

This is the description for "Missile Attack:" "Now one of the most popular arcade games is now available for your computer. Defend your cities from death by intercepting the computer's missiles with yours. Great fun and graphics."

This is the description for "Guided Missile:" "If you can't get enough of Missile Command in the arcades, this program is for you. Try to save the cities on the doomed planet from the deadly missiles. Great Graphics and Sound."

----------

Hustle (Version 3.0).
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 9, Side 1.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"You are a snake winding your way through a barren field. As you wander about aimlessly, your stomach begins to growl. Suddenly, gophers pop up from their underground burrows. Eating them will supply you with extra time but will also lengthen your tail. How long can you feast before entangling yourself in a knot? Only $10.00; Gopher it!"

----------

Laser Battle. - NOT YET ARCHIVED
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 10, Side 2.
1981.

In Laser Battle, each of two players tries to destroy the other by piercing through his shield to destroy the other's weapon. Energy $10.00 (per gallon).

----------

Maze-A-Matic.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 4, Side 2.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Your Bally Arcade will draw a simple maze that you must survive; but it is not that easy! Walls will constantly be added to hinder your path."

"Bally draws a maze and you must get through it, but walls are added to block you. You must have skill and luck to get through!!!"

"'Maze-A-Matic' creates a constantly changing maze which you must get through. If you get stuck, you can always 'Hyperspace.'"

----------

Mystery Maze (Version 4.2).
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 9, Side 2.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"In Mystery Maze you must navigate through energy barriers while avoiding storms and fuel thieves."

----------

Nuts-O.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

According to Mike White's list of Astrocade software, this game is on tape 6, but I can find no evidence of that fact.

----------

Reverse.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 6, Side 2.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Reverse is a challenging puzzle which will probably take you many, many hours to master. We know the secret, but will you??"

"Try to reverse all of the numbers so that they are in numerical order. Do it in as few turns or as little time."

----------

Robot Alert! (Version 4.5).
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 3, Side 1.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

This game was later renamed "Robot Alert" (the explanation mark was dropped).

"Yet another fun-filled arcade-type game is adapted to the Bally. You are in a maze-like room and must kill all of the robots before they get you. But, you can never beat this game."

"You have been transported into an alien vessel which is protected by many robots, created for the sole purpose of destroying intruders. You must avoid these robots at all costs (see below). As time goes on, more intelligent robots appear. You may even go berzerk trying to eliminate them all. Costs (see above): $12.00."

----------

Simon Says (Version 3.0).
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 3, Side 2.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"The electronic game of a similar name can now be played on your Bally. Notes will be added to a series which you must repeat."

"In 'Simon Says' the computer plays many different patterns which you must repeat. The ever-increasing sequence is sure to challenge you."

----------

Smack-Up.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 3, Side 1 (SOURCEBOOK, Fall 1980).
Tape 7, Side 1 (SOURCEBOOK, Summer 1982).
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Thar's GOLD in them thar' hills! Unfortunately, thar's also a 300 pound Hit man chasing after you. His boss wants to make sure that none of the gold leaves his private Treasury Office. It is the culmination of the many gifts he has received from years of dedicated service to the country. Do your best to re-appropriate his funds. A steal at: $10.00."

"Combines the skill and action of 'TARG' and 'Head-On,' which are two popular arcade games. You move your car through a series of maze-like passages to run over as many markers as you can while avoiding the drone car."

----------

Space Dock. - NOT YET ARCHIVED
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 11.
1981.

You are the commander of the experimental landing module of the Space Shuttle. The pilot of this type of vehicle must be trained to execute proper docking maneuvers, avoid collisions with satellites and other space debris and deliver cargo swiftly and safely. This simulation takes you to the Shuttle Pilot Landing and Transportation (SPLAT) Center. Your mission: to survive as many landings as you can. Docking Fee: $10.00. Features machine language graphics.

----------

Starship Bally.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 1, Side 1.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

This game was later renamed "Starship Astro."

"Find the enemy and guide your ship so that he is in your sights, and blast him with a photon torpedo."Try to shoot as many of the enemy spaceships as you can. Records high scores and uses graphics.

"Try to shoot as many of the enemy spaceships as you can. Records high scores and uses graphics."

"In 'Starship Astro,' you are the commanding pilot of the most powerful Starship in the galaxy. Your mission is to destroy every threat to the security of your home planet."

----------

Super Craps.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 2, Side 2.
1980.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Try your hand at rolling the dice. Graphic dice are displayed as up to four people bet on the outcome."

"1-4 people can get all the fun of craps without risking a cent. Each player controls his own bank and can bet with or against the roller. Has great graphics!!"

"Up to four people can play 'Super Craps.' Bet on the outcome of the graphic dice. See who can win the most money."

----------

Super Slot.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 1, Side 2.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"The Bally Casino wants you to play its latest slot machine. Up to four players can participate. Great Fun!!"

"Up to four people can play this Great Slot Machine right in your home. Each player controls his own bank. Graphics and sound are used throughout the program."

"'Super Slot' is a four player slot machine. See how long you can keep your money."

----------

Tic-Tac-Dough.
By Super Software (Robert Rosenhouse).
Tape 4, Side 1.
1981.
Archived from a tape in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Based on the game show of the same name. Pick one of nine squares and uncover a money amount, a bonus word, or the Dragon. If you pass $1,000 you win!! Find the dragon and you lose."

"Play the bonus round from this famous game show. Pick from 9 squares to uncover money, TIC, TAC, or the dragon. Get the dragon and you lose. $1,000 wins. Graphics!!!"

"Now you can play the famous game show at home. Pick from nine squares to uncover either money, bonus words, or the dragon."

18376:
I already knew that "Starship Bally" and "Super Slot" were slow (see my message from August 15, 2019, below).  I played them again this evening and took some screenshots.  "Starship Bally" is just a timed shooter (and a boring one at that) and with "Super Slot," I couldn't figure out how to change how much money I would pluck down with each spin, making them game feel non-interactive.

Oh, and playing these games on real hardware (the only way to play 300-baud games) is a delight-- as I love to play with the under-used-- in this home, anyway-- 300-baud tape interface.

Bob Rosenhouse REALLY got better at making his games, as his game "Lazer Blazer" is fast and fun as opposed to these two games from Tape 1, which are slow and clunky.  However, these types of games are what everyone was able to create with Bally BASIC in 1980 before the techies started working out how to speed-up BASIC.  Both of these two games are extremely early examples of playing around with Bally BASIC; remember, the language wasn't available until September of 1978.  Tricks were only just beginning to trickle into the Arcadian in 1979 and 1980.  It wasn't until the release of AstroBASIC that game design really started to speed up and advance.  It was with the introduction of games which used the machine language subroutines built into the Bally's on-board 8K ROM that games really started to, literally, accelerate.

I like these early Super Software games, for they each give us an example of the early steps of the Bally BASIC home programmers.  Without the spread of information through the Bally Arcade newsletters, the rough drafts would have remained about as advanced as games got on the Astrocade.

Adam

It has been a while since I explored any 300-baud Bally BASIC games.  I thought I might explore the library of Super Software, BASIC software that was written by Bob Rosenhouse:

I really don't know anything about this company except that they released 14 tapes, as shown in these four pages of ads from the Summer 1982 issue of The Sourcebook:

https://ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/sourcebooks/Sourcebook_1982_Summer.pdf#79

I loaded the two programs on the first tape on real hardware.  The first one, Starship Bally, is SLOW.  It looks okay though.  The second program, Super Slot, sure is boring.  It reminded me of when Paul and I talked on the Astrocast podcast about the many, many slot machine programs for the astrocade.  This one is extremely simple.

I didn't realize until today that there are some programs not archived from the Super Software library.  I looked around; I guess they just aren't available.  Plus, as far as I can tell, none of the AstroBASIC versions of the software have been archived at all.  I also can't find any documentation for any of these games.

I recorded videos of me playing these two games.  I had planned to add some commentary and then upload them to YouTube.  They're extremely simple looking and I debated whether or not I would upload them at all.  I think I may just upload them as plain videos without commentary.  They're not good (or even fun) examples of BASIC programs for the Bally, but they're great examples of, I suppose, the sort of BASIC programs that many people would try to write.

Starship Bally - 2000-Baud Conversion
October 6, 2021

Included is Super Software's 300-baud version of "Starship Bally" in a zipped file.  It has been converted to 2000-baud format using the 300-baud to 2000-baud conversion utility in the AstroBASIC manual.  I used BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4 to archive the RAW WAV file so that it will load and run under AstroBASIC.  I've also attached the BASIC listing of the program as output from wBallyBin.  The BASIC output was saved as a Word document.

I have loaded "Starship Bally" into the Windows 64-bit version of MAME 0.218. I played the game once without issues.  I have attached a screenshot of the game as it looks when running under emulation.  Of course, it also loads fine on a real Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

I removed the :RETURN from line 8, which causes AstroBASIC to crash.  I aso changed lines 8 and 510 so that NT=0 is now NT=-1.  This makes the sound work with AstroBASIC-- but it still isn't quite right.  I didn't troubleshoot the sound any more than this quick value change to NT.

As expected, "Starship Bally" plays faster when run under AstroBASIC.

When playing the game using Bally BASIC, the games has not crashed on me.  When I played it using AstroBASIC, the game has crashed on line 115.  This is that line:

115 BOX X,Y,40,4,1;BOX X,Y,38,6,1;BOX X,Y,36,8,1;BOX X,Y+6,20,4,1

I seem to remember that AstroBASIC does some range checking for LINE and BOX commands that Bally BASIC doesn't do.  Perhaps AstroBASIC is running into variables that are out of range on this line.  I didn't check into this issue either.

I made this 2000-baud conversion for Ken Lill.  He called me this morning.  He wants to play with and clean-up this game's BASIC code; he hopes to make it run faster.

These 2000-baud conversions take quite a bit of time to create.  I don't do them often, as the required steps are many and I need to bounce from one computer to another over various steps.  Still, I hope that Ken and others can give this game a whirl now that it runs under emulation.  This game plays slowly (VERY slowly), but it's easy to see that the programmer was just learning to make games in Bally BASIC.

Have fun!

Adam

The printers back then couldn't print the multiply sign (at least not easily through the Bally BASIC kludge printer interface).  Thus, a lowercase "b" is the multiply sign.  So, the previous line would be (where my lowercase x is the multiply sign):

RND(11)x5-35

Mindbender (reverse Space Sleuth)
Two copies of program. No apparent differences. Processed well.

Space Sleuth (reverse Mind Bender)
Two loads, first is an intro graphic, second is the main program. I needed to make a second recording to get the main program to process correctly. The intro graphic sets up the main program to load automatically, but there doesn't seem to be enough of a delay on the tape for this to work without pausing. I added some extra silence to the processed version to make this work without pausing. The answers are displayed in a difficult to read color scheme that you're supposed to use some red cellophane that came with the instructions to read.

10A Side 1
Tape was originally Elvis' Worldwide Gold Award Hits, but all music has been erased. The tape has a number of 2000 baud loads. Some of these don't work correctly despite seeming to process without errors. They may be unsuccessful attempts to copy the programs. I'm not uploading processed versions when we already have a version archived from a commercial tape.
Part 1 -- Exitor's Revenge by L&M Software -- works
Part 2 -- Alien Invasion title screen by L&M Software -- works
Part 3 -- Alien Invasion main program by L&M Software -- works 
Part 4 -- very short, sounds like it might have data, but won't process and doesn't seem likely to be a complete program
Part 5 -- The Gate Escape Side 1 by WaveMakers -- doesn't work
Part 6 -- also The Gate Escape Side 1 by WaveMakers -- works
Part 7 -- Exitor's Revenge by L&M Software -- didnt' process correctly
Part 8 -- Lookout For The Bull by WaveMakers -- works
Part 9 -- extremely short, sounds like just a header tone, ignoring
Part 10 -- The Guard
This hasn't been positively identified, but it does resemble the description of Super Software's Crossfire: "Crossfire challenges you to gather all of the energy units that are being guarded by the malicious laser beams. The player must beware of the deadly crossfiring beams."
The program flashes "The Guard" in large font at the start, so that's what I'm calling it. You can move the character sprite up and down with the joystick. The screen wraps at the top and bottom. You can fire left or right with the joystick. Enemies approach from the side, which you can shoot to gain oxygen. Sometimes lasers fire at you from the side. Occasionally, obstacles pop up along your path that you have to avoid, or more helpfully extra oxygen pickups. You lose a life when you get hit or run out of oxygen.
Part 11 -- Lazer Blazer (machine language graphics version) by Super Software
Thanks to Adam Trionfo for identifying this. Lazer Blazer was printed in Arcadian volume 5 issue 6, which also advertised a machine language graphics version for sale. This is the commercial version. The gameplay is similar to Laser Blast for the Atari 2600.
"Lazer Blazer is a game of skill. The object is to destroy each of the lazer outposts before being hit yourself. The game uses joystick one. To move your spaceship, move the joystick in that direction. To fire straight down, pull the trigger. To fire at an angle, pull the trigger AND move the joystick at the same time. The first round consists of three bases. When you destroy all of them, you will receive bonus points, and will go on to the next round. If you take too long to complete a round, you will hear a warning sound. After the warning sound, you will only have a few seconds with which to hit the remaining base(s). Each game consists of three turns, with a bonus turn awarded at each interval of 2,500 points.
"The graphics in this game are simple 'BOX' graphics. A version of this game complete with machine language graphics is available from SUPER SOFTWARE for only $6.00.
"GOOD LUCK!!!"

Part 13 -- also Exitors Revenge by L&M Software -- doesn't work
Part 14 -- also Exitors Revenge by L&M Software -- doesn't work
Part 15 -- Exitor's Revenge title screen -- works
Part 16 -- Exitor's Revenge -- doesn't work

Two copies, both work.

108187 (embossed on tape, no other label)
One side has 7 2000 baud segments, the other is blank.
I had the most luck processing these after applying a bandpass filter.
These tend to be newsletter programs, and have just random text on the title screens. As we already have better copies of these, I haven't uploaded processed versions.

Two copies. Not binary identical, but no apparent differences. Processes well. Having trouble actually completing the game, as I did with the 300 baud version. This is sometimes called Coyote Roadrunner Desert Race, but since both the tape and program merely say Coyote Roadrunner, I've went with that title.

Atom Smasher (reverse Coyote Roadrunner)
Two copies. Not binary identical, but no apparent differences. Processes well.

L&M Demo (reverse Alien Invasion)
Tape dated 1984, but the programs advertised released 1982, and both demos give copyright 1982.
Part 1 -- Nautilus Demo

I didn't have any problems saving the attachment. It's just a text file that can be opened in Notepad etc. It would definitely need cleaned up to work with the 300 baud utility programs like txt2prg. Bally BASIC has keywords as part of the character set to save memory, so something like "PRINT" is a single character, not the letters P-R-I-N-T. txt2prg handles this by using the word in lower case followed by a space -- "print ". my first pass at getting this ready for evaluation has proven to be interesting. First of all, it was written in 1980, the Bally was still an infant, The programming hints that were in Cursor, Basic Express and the Acadian were still just getting started. For this reason, I really can't fault most bad programming.However, the 3 things that slow Bally basic programs down the most are 
1) GOSUB   2) GOTO and 3) IF statements.

GOSUB and GOTO start looking for the line that is being accessed by starting fro the start of the program (I.E. line 1 or 10) and go through every byte looking for the matchng line.When you put your subroutines near the end, BASIC goes through the entire program looking for the number EACH TIME.
IFstatements have to be evaluated through a part of the BASIC called "evaluate expression" whch also look at any math in that part. The IF taes quite a bit longer than the speeded math. 

say you have this:
100 IF X>10IF X<100 GOTO 120110 GOTO 10120 .....
That could be done like this:110 IF (X<11)x(X>99)GOTO 10
Go ahead, test it outThe 1st takes 22 bytes and has to evaluate 2 IF statements, the 2nd has 20 bytes and only has to eveluate 1 IF
    On Wednesday, October 6, 2021, 03:30:30 PM EDT, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:  
 
 Starship Bally - 2000-Baud Conversion
October 6, 2021

Included is Super Software's 300-baud version of "Starship Bally" in a zipped file.  It has been converted to 2000-baud format using the 300-baud to 2000-baud conversion utility in the AstroBASIC manual.  I used BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4 to archive the RAW WAV file so that it will load and run under AstroBASIC.  I've also attached the BASIC listing of the program as output from wBallyBin.  The BASIC output was saved as a Word document.

I have loaded "Starship Bally" into the Windows 64-bit version of MAME 0.218. I played the game once without issues.  I have attached a screenshot of the game as it looks when running under emulation.  Of course, it also loads fine on a real Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

I removed the :RETURN from line 8, which causes AstroBASIC to crash.  I aso changed lines 8 and 510 so that NT=0 is now NT=-1.  This makes the sound work with AstroBASIC-- but it still isn't quite right.  I didn't troubleshoot the sound any more than this quick value change to NT.

As expected, "Starship Bally" plays faster when run under AstroBASIC.

When playing the game using Bally BASIC, the games has not crashed on me.  When I played it using AstroBASIC, the game has crashed on line 115.  This is that line:

115 BOX X,Y,40,4,1;BOX X,Y,38,6,1;BOX X,Y,36,8,1;BOX X,Y+6,20,4,1

I seem to remember that AstroBASIC does some range checking for LINE and BOX commands that Bally BASIC doesn't do.  Perhaps AstroBASIC is running into variables that are out of range on this line.  I didn't check into this issue either.

I made this 2000-baud conversion for Ken Lill.  He called me this morning.  He wants to play with and clean-up this game's BASIC code; he hopes to make it run faster.

These 2000-baud conversions take quite a bit of time to create.  I don't do them often, as the required steps are many and I need to bounce from one computer to another over various steps.  Still, I hope that Ken and others can give this game a whirl now that it runs under emulation.  This game plays slowly (VERY slowly), but it's easy to see that the programmer was just learning to make games in Bally BASIC.

Have fun!

Adam

my first pass at getting this ready for evaluation has proven to be interesting. First of all, it was written in 1980, the Bally was still an infant, The programming hints that were in Cursor, Basic Express and the Acadian were still just getting started. For this reason, I really can't fault most bad programming.
However, the 3 things that slow Bally basic programs down the most are
1) GOSUB   2) GOTO and 3) IF statements.

GOSUB and GOTO start looking for the line that is being accessed by starting fro the start of the program (I.E. line 1 or 10) and go through every byte looking for the matchng line.
When you put your subroutines near the end, BASIC goes through the entire program looking for the number EACH TIME.

IFstatements have to be evaluated through a part of the BASIC called "evaluate expression" whch also look at any math in that part. The IF taes quite a bit longer than the speeded math.

say you have this:

100 IF X>10IF X<100 GOTO 120
110 GOTO 10
120 .....

That could be done like this:
110 IF (X<11)x(X>99)GOTO 10

Go ahead, test it out
The 1st takes 22 bytes and has to evaluate 2 IF statements, the 2nd has 20 bytes and only has to eveluate 1 IF

Included is Super Software's 300-baud version of "Starship Bally" in a zipped file.  It has been converted to 2000-baud format using the 300-baud to 2000-baud conversion utility in the AstroBASIC manual.  I used BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4 to archive the RAW WAV file so that it will load and run under AstroBASIC.  I've also attached the BASIC listing of the program as output from wBallyBin.  The BASIC output was saved as a Word document.

I have loaded "Starship Bally" into the Windows 64-bit version of MAME 0.218. I played the game once without issues.  I have attached a screenshot of the game as it looks when running under emulation.  Of course, it also loads fine on a real Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

I removed the :RETURN from line 8, which causes AstroBASIC to crash.  I aso changed lines 8 and 510 so that NT=0 is now NT=-1.  This makes the sound work with AstroBASIC-- but it still isn't quite right.  I didn't troubleshoot the sound any more than this quick value change to NT.

As expected, "Starship Bally" plays faster when run under AstroBASIC.

When playing the game using Bally BASIC, the games has not crashed on me.  When I played it using AstroBASIC, the game has crashed on line 115.  This is that line:

115 BOX X,Y,40,4,1;BOX X,Y,38,6,1;BOX X,Y,36,8,1;BOX X,Y+6,20,4,1

I seem to remember that AstroBASIC does some range checking for LINE and BOX commands that Bally BASIC doesn't do.  Perhaps AstroBASIC is running into variables that are out of range on this line.  I didn't check into this issue either.

I made this 2000-baud conversion for Ken Lill.  He called me this morning.  He wants to play with and clean-up this game's BASIC code; he hopes to make it run faster.

These 2000-baud conversions take quite a bit of time to create.  I don't do them often, as the required steps are many and I need to bounce from one computer to another over various steps.  Still, I hope that Ken and others can give this game a whirl now that it runs under emulation.  This game plays slowly (VERY slowly), but it's easy to see that the programmer was just learning to make games in Bally BASIC.

First of all, it was written in 1980, the Bally was still an infant, The programming hints that were in Cursor, Basic Express and the Acadian were still just getting started. For this reason, I really can't fault most bad programming.
However, the 3 things that slow Bally basic programs down the most are
1) GOSUB  2) GOTO and 3) IF statements.

GOSUB and GOTO start looking for the line that is being accessed by starting fro the start of the program (I.E. line 1 or 10) and go through every byte looking for the matchng line.
When you put your subroutines near the end, BASIC goes through the entire program looking for the number EACH TIME.

IFstatements have to be evaluated through a part of the BASIC called "evaluate expression" whch also look at any math in that part. The IF taes quite a bit longer than the speeded math.

say you have this:

100 IF X>10IF X<100 GOTO 120
110 GOTO 10
120 .....

That could be done like this:
110 IF (X<11)x(X>99)GOTO 10

Go ahead, test it out
The 1st takes 22 bytes and has to evaluate 2 IF statements, the 2nd has 20 bytes and only has to eveluate 1 IF

115 BOX X,Y,40,4,1;BOX X,Y,38,6,1;BOX X,Y,36,8,1;BOX X,Y+6,20,4,1

Have fun!

Adam

Yes, the source code for Palo Alto Tiny BASIC is well-documented, which is why I, I've always thought, that Jay Fenton used it as the starting point for Bally BASIC.  Sure, Tiny BASIC's small footprint fit the requirements, to some degree, of the Bally Home Library Computer (4K of RAM, anyone?), but Jay was also pressed for time.  I wonder how much of the 8080's source code made into into the Z80 assembly listing.  I've always wanted to compare parts of the code to check ever since I read a letter written to Bob Fabris in about 1978 or 1979, where the writer said that it was reading the source code for PATB that taught him some of the ins and outs of Bally BASIC.

Adam
