I added an alternate version of "Checkers" by W&W Software Sales (Bob Weber). This 300-BAUD, Bally BASIC program was released in 1979 on Tape 4 as program 2.

This one player checkers program uses the hand controller to control the game. Double and triple jumps are controlled automatically.

You can download the game for the Astrocade, here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/w&w_software_sales/w&w_software_sales.html#CheckersWandWSoftwareBB

Instructions

Uses hand controller.  The 8 positions of the joystick are used to move the flashing square from one square to the next.  Position the flashing square on the checker you want to move, pull the trigger until the flashing square shuts itself off momentarily.  Then position the flashing square on the next square you wish to move to, pull the trigger again and the computer will move your checker.  In the case of a double jump, only make the first part of the jump, the computer will automatically jump the second checker; and the same on a triple jump.  When the computer is ready to make his move, it will make a noise, and after it has moved the flashing square will indicate the piece it moved or jumped.  1 player.

Archiving Notes:

- These program directions were transcribed from a printout on carbon paper of the instructions for W&W Software Sales, Tapes 1-7.  The seven pages faded by the time the pages were scanned in September of 2021.  This set of instructions can be downloaded here:

https://ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/misc/misc.html#WandWSoftwareSalesTapeInstructions

- Checkers (1979)(W&W Software Sales)(300 baud)[a] -  This was archived from the Paul Zibits collection in August/October 2021 by Paul Thacker.  He notes, "Slightly different version than previously archived program."

I encourage you to give this checkers game a try; it's rather fun and doesn't take as long as I expected to make a move.  It hasn't been archived for AstroBASIC and it would probably make a good candidate to be converted to this slightly faster BASIC.  I suppose the sound would need to be changed, but I think that the program would mostly work as-is.

Load it up and... have fun!

Adam

I added an alternate version of "Cylon Raiders" by W&W Software Sales (Bob Weber) to BallyAlley.com. This 300-BAUD, Bally BASIC program was released in 1979 on Tape 4 as program 1.

You can download the game for the Astrocade, here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/w&w_software_sales/w&w_software_sales.html#CylonRaidersWandWSoftwareBB

The BASIC listings for the main and an alternate version of "Cylon Raiders" are below.

Instructions

Uses hand controller.  You are in a viper and the crosshairs on your scope are moved with the 8 positions of the joystick.  When the Cylon is in the center of your scope you pull the trigger to shoot him down.  One Player.

Play Notes

Today, I played the main archive of this game: Cylon Raiders (1979)(W&W Software Sales)(300 baud). After I destroyed a few aliens, my Viper was destroyed and the game-screen went black.  There didn't appear to be any way to restart or quite the game (HALT didn't work).  I had to shut the Bally Arcade off and turn it back on again to get back to Bally BASIC.  I'm not sure why this happened or if it's normal behavior for this game.

Archiving Notes:

There are alternate versions of this program; I'm not sure of the differences between each of them, but here are some brief notes about them.

- Cylon Raiders (mod) (19xx)(W&W Software Sales and unknown author)(300 baud).zip and Cylon Raiders (mod) (19xx)(W&W Software Sales and unknown author)(300 baud)[a].zip - Archived May 31, 2013 by Paul Thacker from tape in Brett Bilbrey's collection. There are several code changes from the published version of Cylon Raiders. The two mods only differ from each other in the first couple of lines.

- Cylon Raiders (1979)(W&W Software Sales)(300 baud)[a] - This was archived from the Paul Zibits collection in August/October 2021 by Paul Thacker.  He notes, "Slightly different version than previously archived program, doesn't include "TEMP CRITICAL" printout."

This is another game that plays okay for such an early example of a Bally BASIC game.  It's too bad the main archived version seemed to crash when I played it.

Thanks for continuing to archive all of these BASIC games, Paul!  I've been having a wonderful time over this last week archiving at least one game a day.  These BASIC programs can be quirky; that's why I like them.

Enjoy!

Adam

I added an alternate version of "Checkers" by W&W Software Sales (Bob Weber). This 300-BAUD, Bally BASIC program was released in 1979 on Tape 4 as program 2.

This one player checkers program uses the hand controller to control the game. Double and triple jumps are controlled automatically.

You can download the game for the Astrocade, here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/w&w_software_sales/w&w_software_sales.html#CheckersWandWSoftwareBB

Instructions

Uses hand controller.  The 8 positions of the joystick are used to move the flashing square from one square to the next.  Position the flashing square on the checker you want to move, pull the trigger until the flashing square shuts itself off momentarily.  Then position the flashing square on the next square you wish to move to, pull the trigger again and the computer will move your checker.  In the case of a double jump, only make the first part of the jump, the computer will automatically jump the second checker; and the same on a triple jump.  When the computer is ready to make his move, it will make a noise, and after it has moved the flashing square will indicate the piece it moved or jumped.  1 player.

Archiving Notes:

- These program directions were transcribed from a printout on carbon paper of the instructions for W&W Software Sales, Tapes 1-7.  The seven pages faded by the time the pages were scanned in September of 2021.  This set of instructions can be downloaded here:

https://ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/misc/misc.html#WandWSoftwareSalesTapeInstructions

- Checkers (1979)(W&W Software Sales)(300 baud)[a] -  This was archived from the Paul Zibits collection in August/October 2021 by Paul Thacker.  He notes, "Slightly different version than previously archived program."

I encourage you to give this checkers game a try; it's rather fun and doesn't take as long as I expected to make a move.  It hasn't been archived for AstroBASIC and it would probably make a good candidate to be converted to this slightly faster BASIC.  I suppose the sound would need to be changed, but I think that the program would mostly work as-is.

Load it up and... have fun!

Adam

Allen Schweitzer asked Michael Matte some advice about testing an Astrocade power supply.  Allen wondered if the AC adapter is repairable.  Michael gave some great advice, which I'm sharing here.

Adam

----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Sunday, September 19, 2021
Subject: bally ac adapter

TESTING THE BLACK ASTROCADE POWER TRANSFORMER (XFMR) THAT PLUGS INTO AN 120VAC WALL OUTLET

You CAN test the black xfmr without it being plugged into a motherboard. The ac voltage ratings are stamped on the xfmr plastic housing. I'm looking at a xfmr right now and its ratings are:

center winding, red to green, 1 amp, 7.5vac
2 end windings, black to red and also green to white, 85 ma, 10.8vac

Since the end windings are symmetrical, it doesn't matter which way you connect the color coded plug into the motherboard. I always connect this plug to the motherboard with its metal contacts up, so I can see there is a good connection to the motherboard ac pins.

I'm not sure if all the black xfmrs always had these same 2 output voltages.

If you are not getting ac voltages that are close to these 2 ratings, the xfmr is junk. Try your ac voltmeter on a known working xfmr so you know your ac voltmeter is reasonably accurate.

You can also use an ohmmeter on an unplugged xfmr to check for a break (open) in the primary or its 3 secondary windings. If there is no break in the winding, the ohmmeter will read very low resistance, probably less than 1 ohm. If a xfmr overheats because of a motherboard short or near short, the primary winding may burn out. You might even here a "pop" when that happens.

If you can't get your hands on a power xfmr replacement, a power xfmr substitution can be built, if you have the expertise. Reference MCM Design's Power Transformer Substitution on the BallyAlley.com website.

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/faqs.html#AstrocadePowerTransformerSubstitution

Bye.
MCM

18498:
Hmm, I think that "bit-rot" only refers to EPROMs/EEPROMS.  Certainly there are non-computer systems (radios and TVs, for instance) that use chips and transistors that go back to the early 1960s that still works today.

I've read that integrated circuits can last, supposedly, maybe 100 years, maybe a thousand years, when they're kept under good conditions.  Of course, most of these computers and game systems that we're talking about are kept in terrible conditions.  You'll find them in sheds.  Garages.  Heck, even in New Mexico landfills.  The IC only dates back to around 1960, so we can't test real-world conditions to know for sure how long they'll last.  I remember in the 1980s reading that CDs would last forever.  That turns out to be completely wrong.  Probably the same is true about everything we've read about the lifespan of ICs.

I presume that "Raikusu's" figure of "50 years" is probably a good estimate of an ICs lifespan.  Surely, I've seen chips in Venice, California (a suburb of L.A., near the Pacific Ocean) on an Amiga 3000 in the early 2000s that literally had legs of the ICs rusted off of them.  At the time, those ICs were only about ten years old.

Maybe all classic computer and game system users should do what I do whenever I turn on my Astrocade.  Cross your fingers.  Pray.  Do whatever suits your fancy.  Above all-- have hope that the machine will last forever and don't tell the hardware how old it is today.  Maybe if the hardware thinks that it's still young then it will hang on just a little longer.

Adam
